Memory Jogger.new: For a 4--3 Court, Chief Justice Marshall held that Missouri's interest-bearing loan-office certificates, issued on the faith of the state and designed to circulate as money, were unconstitutional ``bills of credit'' under Article I, Section 10, even though they were not legal tender, so a note given for them was void (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/29/410/}{Justia}).

Examples: Future Applications.src: Facing a severe budget impasse, the State of Ozark enacts a statute directing its State Treasurer to print \$500 million in ``Fiscal Liquidity Certificates'' in \$5, \$20, and \$100 bearer denominations. The certificates are not legal tender for private debts, but they are receivable at face value for all state taxes and public-university tuition, and the statute pledges ``the full faith and credit of the State of Ozark'' for redemption in five years.

Unconstitutional under \textit{Craig}. Even without private legal-tender status or the label ``bills of credit,'' the certificates are issued directly by state officers, backed by the state's faith, and structured in small bearer denominations to circulate as a common medium of exchange.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Unconstitutional): Interest-Bearing Scrip Backed by a Dedicated Fund.} During a cash shortage, a State's comptroller pays state employees and contractors with interest-bearing scrip in \$1, \$5, and \$10 denominations, payable to bearer and receivable for all state taxes and fees. The statute pledges the revenue of the state lottery to redeem the scrip within three years. The State argues that interest makes the scrip's value fluctuate and that a dedicated fund, not bare state credit, stands behind it. Those were the arguments of Justices Johnson and Thompson in dissent, and the \textit{Craig} majority rejected them: Missouri's certificates also bore interest and rested on a pledged fund. Because the scrip is issued directly by state officers in small denominations designed to circulate as money, it is a prohibited bill of credit.

\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Constitutional): Ordinary State Bonds Sold to Investors.} To finance highway construction, a State sells \$800 million in twenty-year general-obligation bonds in \$5,000 denominations to banks, pension funds, and other investors, pledging its full faith and credit to repay them with interest. A taxpayer argues that paper issued on the faith of the State is a bill of credit under \textit{Craig}. The argument fails. Marshall explained that the Bills of Credit Clause does not bar ordinary state borrowing or contracts to pay for goods and services; it forbids paper intended to circulate through the community for its ordinary purposes as money. Large-denomination investment bonds are a loan to the State, not a medium of exchange, so they are not bills of credit even though they rest on the State's credit.

\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Constitutional Under \textit{Briscoe}): Notes of a State-Owned Corporate Bank.} A State charters a bank, owned entirely by the State and governed by directors chosen by the legislature, that can sue and be sued in its own name. The bank lends its own small-denomination notes to borrowers, and the notes circulate as currency; they are redeemable from the bank's own capital and are not issued on the faith of the State. Under \textit{Briscoe v.\ Bank of Commonwealth of Kentucky}, 36 U.S.\ (11 Pet.) 257 (1837), the notes are not bills of credit because a separately incorporated, suable entity issues them on its own corporate funds. Justice Story's \textit{Briscoe} dissent, invoking \textit{Craig}'s rule that the Constitution prohibits things rather than names, would treat them as an indirect emission, but \textit{Briscoe} remains the governing rule.

Examples: Future Applications.src: By contrast, suppose the State of Frontier charters an independent, suable public corporation to issue ``Frontier Digital Dollars''---blockchain tokens redeemable on demand for \$1.00 U.S., backed 102\% by segregated U.S. dollars and short-term Treasury bills held in trust, with an explicit statutory disclaimer that neither the state's general faith nor its taxing power backs the tokens.

Under \textit{Briscoe} and \textit{Houston \& Texas Central}, the tokens likely survive Article I, Section 10 scrutiny because they are issued by a separately suable corporate instrumentality, backed by a dedicated, fully liquid reserve fund rather than sovereign credit, and redeemable on demand. Conversely, a functionalist challenger invoking Marshall's ``names, and not things'' principle in \textit{Craig} and Story's \textit{Briscoe} dissent would argue that a state-created, state-governed entity minting a circulating digital medium designed for everyday commerce and taxes is an impermissible indirect emission of bills of credit.

Examples: Future Applications.new: The Court has never applied \textit{Craig} or \textit{Briscoe} to a digital instrument, so which line controls is uncertain.
